variants.stem: Moving down a group of the periodic table, what happens to atomic radius?
As you move down Group 1 from lithium to potassium, the size of the atoms:
Atoms get larger going down a group because they have more of what?
Why does atomic radius increase from the top of a group to the bottom?
Which statement describes the trend in atomic size down a column of the periodic table?
opts: Atomic size is unrelated to position

variants.stem: Compared with a sodium atom, a potassium atom is:
Going from fluorine to chlorine to bromine, atomic radius:
A student compares atoms in the same group. As the period number goes up, the atoms:

questions.why: Atomic radius increases down a group because each lower period adds another electron shell, putting the outer electrons farther from the nucleus.
questions.deep: Trends: atomic radius increases down a group and decreases from left to right across a period (more protons pull the shells in tighter). Electronegativity and ionization energy generally follow the opposite pattern: they increase up a group and across a period.

variants.stem: Which group of elements contains the most reactive metals?
Lithium, sodium, and potassium belong to which group?
Which elements have a single valence electron and react vigorously with water?
Elements in Group 1 of the periodic table are called:
Which group of metals readily loses one electron to form 1+ ions?
Which family of elements is stored under oil because it reacts with air and water?
Which family of elements includes sodium and potassium?
The most reactive metals are found in which group?

questions.why: The alkali metals (Group 1) have one valence electron that they lose very easily, which makes them the most reactive metals.
questions.deep: Reactivity of alkali metals increases down the group (Li < Na < K < Rb < Cs) because the outer electron is farther from the nucleus and easier to lose. Group 2 (alkaline earth metals) are reactive but less so; Group 17 (halogens) are the most reactive nonmetals; Group 18 (noble gases) are unreactive.

variants.stem: How many valence electrons do the alkaline earth metals (Group 2) have?
Magnesium and calcium are in Group 2. How many valence electrons does each atom have?
Elements in Group 2 tend to lose how many electrons to form ions?
A calcium atom has how many electrons in its outer shell?
Beryllium, magnesium, and calcium all share which number of valence electrons?
How many valence electrons are in an atom of barium (Group 2)?
To reach a stable octet configuration, Group 2 atoms lose how many electrons?
Group 2 on the periodic table corresponds to how many valence electrons?

questions.why: Group 2 (the alkaline earth metals) elements have 2 valence electrons, which they lose to form 2+ ions.
questions.deep: For the main groups, the group number (1, 2) or its last digit (13–18) gives the valence electrons: Group 1 → 1, Group 2 → 2, Group 13 → 3, Group 14 → 4, Group 15 → 5, Group 16 → 6, Group 17 → 7, Group 18 → 8. Group 2 atoms lose 2 electrons: Mg → Mg²⁺, Ca → Ca²⁺.

variants.stem: A chlorine atom has 17 protons. It gains one electron to form Cl⁻. How many electrons does the Cl⁻ ion have? Give a whole number.
An ion of chlorine has 17 protons and a 1− charge. How many electrons does it have? Give a whole number.
Cl⁻ is formed from a neutral atom with 17 protons. How many electrons are in one Cl⁻ ion? Give a whole number.
An anion has 17 protons and a charge of −1. How many electrons does it have? Give a whole number.
How many electrons are in an ion that has 17 protons and a net charge of 1−? Give a whole number.
A neutral atom with atomic number 17 gains 1 electron. How many electrons does it now have? Give a whole number.
The chloride ion has an atomic number of 17. How many electrons does it contain? Give a whole number.
Chlorine (atomic number 17) forms a 1− ion. How many electrons does this ion have? Give a whole number.

questions.why: A neutral chlorine atom has 17 electrons. Gaining one electron to form Cl⁻ gives 17 + 1 = 18 electrons.
questions.deep: Electrons = protons − charge. For Cl⁻: 17 − (−1) = 18. The protons stay at 17 because the atom is still chlorine. Cl⁻ now has 18 electrons, the same as argon, a stable full-shell configuration.

variants.stem: What is the term for a solid changing directly into a gas without becoming a liquid?
Dry ice (solid CO₂) turns directly into carbon dioxide gas at room pressure. This process is called:
Which phase change skips the liquid state when going from solid to gas?
Moth balls slowly disappear without melting. Which process is occurring?
Snow slowly vanishing on a cold, dry, windy day without melting is an example of:
Which term describes the transition from solid directly to gas?
Which phase change occurs when particles in a solid gain enough energy to escape directly as a gas?
Which process is the opposite of deposition?

questions.why: Sublimation is the phase change in which a solid becomes a gas without passing through the liquid state.
questions.deep: Phase changes: melting (solid → liquid), freezing (liquid → solid), vaporization/evaporation (liquid → gas), condensation (gas → liquid), sublimation (solid → gas), deposition (gas → solid). Melting, vaporization, and sublimation absorb energy (endothermic); freezing, condensation, and deposition release energy.

variants.stem: Temperature is a measure of which property of the particles in a substance?
When a substance is heated and its temperature rises, which quantity of its particles increases on average?
Which quantity do particles in warm water have more of, on average, than particles in cold water?
The kinetic molecular theory relates temperature to which property of particles?
Which statement describes particles in a hot object compared with a cold object?
Temperature measures the average:
Heating a gas makes its particles move faster. This means the average ____ of the particles has increased.
What happens to the average kinetic energy of particles when temperature rises?

questions.why: Temperature is a measure of the average kinetic energy of the particles in a substance. Higher temperature means the particles move faster on average.
questions.deep: Heat is the energy transferred between objects because of a temperature difference; temperature is the average kinetic energy of particles. At absolute zero (0 K), particle motion is at its minimum. States of matter: particles in solids vibrate in place, in liquids slide past each other, and in gases move freely.

variants.stem: In a solution made by dissolving salt in water, which substance is the solvent?
Sugar is dissolved in water. Which is the solvent?
Copper sulfate crystals are dissolved in water to make a blue solution. Which substance is the solvent?
Salt is dissolved in water to make saline. The solvent is:
In ocean water, which substance is the solvent that dissolves the salts?
A powdered drink mix is dissolved in water. Which is the solvent?
Which substance does the dissolving in a solution of salt and water?
In a salt-water solution, the substance present in the greater amount that does the dissolving is the:

questions.why: The solvent is the substance that does the dissolving and is usually present in the larger amount. In salt water, water is the solvent and salt is the solute.
questions.deep: Solution = solute + solvent. Water is called the universal solvent because it dissolves so many substances. A solution is a homogeneous mixture: the solute is evenly distributed and does not settle out. Dissolving is a physical change.

variants.stem: Which pH value indicates a basic solution?
Which of these solutions is basic?
Household ammonia is a base. Which pH would you expect?
A solution has a pH above 7. Which value could it be?
Which pH value belongs to a solution with more OH⁻ than H⁺?
Which solution would turn red litmus paper blue?
Which pH is the most basic of these values?
On the pH scale, which value represents a base?

questions.why: A pH above 7 is basic (alkaline). pH 11 has more hydroxide ions (OH⁻) than hydrogen ions (H⁺).
questions.deep: pH below 7 = acidic, pH 7 = neutral (pure water), pH above 7 = basic. Examples: stomach acid ≈ 2, lemon juice ≈ 2, blood ≈ 7.4, baking soda ≈ 9, ammonia ≈ 11, bleach ≈ 13. Bases turn red litmus blue; acids turn blue litmus red.

variants.stem: What are the products of a neutralization reaction between an acid and a base?
HCl + NaOH → ? Which products form?
When an acid and a base react completely, which substances are formed?
Which pair forms when hydrochloric acid reacts with sodium hydroxide?
Antacids neutralize stomach acid. What types of products form in an acid–base neutralization?
Acid + base → ?
Which substances are produced when an acid is neutralized by a base?
A neutralization reaction always produces water and what other type of compound?

questions.why: In a neutralization reaction, an acid reacts with a base to form a salt and water: acid + base → salt + water.
questions.deep: Example: HCl + NaOH → NaCl + H₂O. The H⁺ from the acid combines with the OH⁻ from the base to form water, and the leftover ions form the salt. A complete neutralization of a strong acid with a strong base gives a solution near pH 7.

variants.stem: A solution contains 2.0 moles of NaCl in 4.0 L of solution. What is its molarity in mol/L?
What is the molarity of a solution made by dissolving 2.0 mol of solute in enough water to make 4.0 L of solution?
A chemist prepares 4.0 L of solution containing 2.0 mol of KCl. Find the molarity in mol/L.
Calculate the concentration, in mol/L, of a solution with 2.0 mol of sucrose in 4.0 L of solution.
If 4.0 L of solution holds 2.0 moles of dissolved glucose, what is the molarity in M?
Using M = moles ÷ liters, find the molarity of 2.0 mol of solute in 4.0 L of solution.
2.0 moles of solute are dissolved to make a total volume of 4.0 liters. What is the molarity?
A 4.0 L sample of solution contains 2.0 mol of dissolved salt. What is the molarity in mol/L?

questions.why: Molarity = moles of solute ÷ liters of solution = 2.0 mol ÷ 4.0 L = 0.5 M.
questions.deep: M = mol ÷ L. Check the units: the divisor is liters of SOLUTION (not liters of solvent). If you have milliliters, convert to liters first (divide by 1,000). A 0.5 M solution is less concentrated than a 1.0 M solution.

Select all that apply: Which are typical of acid solutions?

questions.why: Acids taste sour, have a pH below 7, release H⁺ in water, and turn blue litmus paper red. Bases feel slippery, taste bitter, have a pH above 7, release OH⁻, and turn red litmus paper blue.
questions.deep: Memory aids: Acids → H⁺, pH below 7, litmus goes red (A for Acid, Alike red). Bases → OH⁻, pH above 7, litmus goes blue, slippery (like soap). Never taste or touch lab chemicals; these properties are for identification in theory only.

variants.stem: Tap the atom in this water molecule that carries the partial negative charge.
Tap the more electronegative atom in this molecule.
Tap the atom that pulls the shared electrons closer to itself.
Tap the atom that attracts the bonding electrons more strongly.
Tap the end of the molecule that is slightly negative (δ⁻).
Tap the atom in H₂O with the greater electronegativity.
Tap the atom whose stronger pull on shared electrons makes the bonds polar.
Tap the atom that the hydrogens of neighboring water molecules are attracted to in hydrogen bonding.

questions.why: Oxygen is much more electronegative than hydrogen, so it pulls the shared electrons toward itself and carries the partial negative charge (δ⁻).
questions.deep: Each hydrogen carries a partial positive charge (δ⁺). This uneven charge makes water polar, and the δ⁺ hydrogens of one water molecule are attracted to the δ⁻ oxygen of another, forming hydrogen bonds. Electronegativity: O is about 3.5; H is about 2.1.

variants.stem: An mRNA codon reads AUG. Which tRNA anticodon pairs with it?
Which anticodon on a tRNA matches the mRNA codon 5′-AUG-3′?
During translation, a tRNA with which anticodon binds to the start codon AUG?
The codon AUG on mRNA is recognized by a tRNA containing which anticodon?
Which sequence is complementary to the mRNA codon AUG?
A ribosome reads the start codon AUG. Which tRNA anticodon base-pairs with it?
What is the anticodon for the codon AUG?
The anticodon of the tRNA that carries methionine is complementary to the codon AUG. What is it?

questions.why: The tRNA anticodon is complementary to the mRNA codon: A pairs with U, U pairs with A, and G pairs with C. So AUG pairs with UAC.
questions.deep: Remember that RNA uses uracil (U) instead of thymine (T), so a tRNA anticodon never contains T. AUG is the start codon and codes for methionine. Codon (on mRNA) and anticodon (on tRNA) pair like a lock and key during translation.

variants.stem: During which phase of the cell cycle is DNA replicated?
Which stage of interphase is when the cell copies its chromosomes?
A cell doubles its DNA content before mitosis. During which phase does this happen?
In which phase does each chromosome become two sister chromatids?
Which phase of the cell cycle comes between G₁ and G₂?
DNA synthesis occurs during which part of interphase?
Which phase of the cell cycle is characterized by DNA replication?
Before mitosis begins, the DNA is copied during which phase?

questions.why: DNA replication occurs during the S (synthesis) phase of interphase, so each chromosome has two identical sister chromatids before mitosis.
questions.deep: Cell cycle: interphase (G₁ = growth, S = DNA synthesis, G₂ = preparation) → M phase (mitosis: prophase, metaphase, anaphase, telophase) → cytokinesis. Memory aid: S = Synthesis (DNA copied).

opts: Movement from high to low concentration without energy
Movement from low to high concentration using ATP
Movement inside a vesicle fused to the membrane

variants.stem: In diffusion, particles move:
opts: From high concentration to low concentration without energy
From low concentration to high concentration using ATP

variants.stem: Oxygen moves into a cell without using energy. Which statement describes this movement?
A drop of dye spreads through water without stirring. This process is driven by:

variants.stem: Which is a feature of passive transport such as diffusion?
opts: It moves substances against a gradient

variants.stem: Which direction do molecules move during diffusion?
Diffusion continues until:
Which condition does NOT apply to diffusion?

questions.why: Diffusion is the passive movement of particles from an area of higher concentration to an area of lower concentration, and it requires no cellular energy.
questions.deep: Passive transport (no ATP): simple diffusion, facilitated diffusion (through channel or carrier proteins), and osmosis (water). Active transport (needs ATP) moves particles against their gradient. Particles keep moving at equilibrium, but with no net change in concentration.

Which organelle lacks ribosomes and is involved in making lipids?

The organelle that synthesizes cholesterol and phospholipids is the:
Which organelle is the main site of lipid synthesis in the cell?
Which type of endoplasmic reticulum has a smooth appearance and makes lipids?

questions.why: The smooth endoplasmic reticulum has no ribosomes and is the site of lipid, phospholipid, and steroid synthesis.
questions.deep: Rough ER (with ribosomes) makes proteins for export or membranes; smooth ER (no ribosomes) makes lipids and steroids, and detoxifies drugs in the liver. The Golgi apparatus modifies, sorts, and packages products from the ER.

variants.stem: What is the main driver of adaptation in natural selection?
opts: Differences in survival and reproduction among individuals

variants.stem: Which statement is true of evolution by natural selection?
opts: Individuals with favorable traits tend to survive and reproduce more
All individuals have equal chances of surviving and reproducing
Traits acquired during life are passed to offspring
Organisms change on purpose to fit the environment

questions.why: In natural selection, individuals with traits that suit their environment are more likely to survive and reproduce, so those traits become more common in the population over generations.
questions.deep: Four parts: variation exists in a population, some variation is heritable, more offspring are produced than can survive, and individuals with favorable traits leave more offspring. Individuals do not evolve; populations do. Traits gained during a lifetime (such as larger muscles) are not inherited.

variants.stem: Select all that apply: Which are functions of the liver?
Select all that apply: Which tasks does the liver perform?
Select all that apply: The liver is important for which of the following?
opts: Producing red blood cells in adults

variants.stem: Select all that apply: Which are NOT functions of the liver?

Select all that apply: Which substances are made by the liver?
Select all that apply: Which functions are associated with the liver?
Select all that apply: The liver helps maintain homeostasis by:

questions.why: The liver makes bile, stores glycogen, vitamins, and iron, makes plasma proteins (such as albumin and clotting factors), and detoxifies drugs and alcohol.
questions.deep: Not liver jobs: insulin and glucagon come from the pancreas, urine from the kidneys, hydrochloric acid from the stomach, thyroxine from the thyroid, and bile concentration from the gallbladder. The liver is the largest internal organ and has a dual blood supply.

variants.stem: Which valve lies between the right atrium and the right ventricle?
Blood flows from the right atrium into the right ventricle through which valve?
Which heart valve has three cusps and prevents backflow into the right atrium?
Which valve closes when the right ventricle contracts to prevent blood from returning to the right atrium?
Which is the right atrioventricular (AV) valve?
The valve that guards the opening between the upper and lower chambers on the right side of the heart is the:
Deoxygenated blood passes from the right atrium to the right ventricle across which valve?
Which valve is also called the right AV valve?

questions.why: The tricuspid valve is the right atrioventricular valve; it separates the right atrium from the right ventricle and prevents backflow.
questions.deep: Valves in blood-flow order: tricuspid (right AV) → pulmonary (semilunar) → lungs → mitral/bicuspid (left AV) → aortic (semilunar) → body. Memory aid: the Tricuspid valve has three cusps and sits on the right side; the left AV valve (mitral/bicuspid) has two.

variants.stem: Where does most reabsorption of water, glucose, and sodium occur in the nephron?
Which nephron structure reabsorbs nearly all of the filtered glucose and amino acids?
After filtration at the glomerulus, most useful solutes are reclaimed in which part of the nephron?
Which part of the nephron follows Bowman's capsule and reabsorbs the largest share of the filtrate?
Which nephron segment has a brush border that increases surface area for reabsorption?
Which nephron segment reabsorbs about two-thirds of the filtered water and sodium?
Glucose normally does not appear in urine because it is reabsorbed in which structure?
Which segment of the nephron is the main site of reabsorption?

questions.why: The proximal convoluted tubule reabsorbs most of the filtered water and sodium and almost all of the glucose and amino acids back into the blood.
questions.deep: Nephron steps: filtration (glomerulus) → reabsorption (mostly proximal tubule) → secretion (tubules) → concentration of urine (loop of Henle and collecting duct, under the control of ADH). Filtration moves things out of the blood; reabsorption moves useful things back in.

variants.stem: Which division of the autonomic nervous system prepares the body for fight or flight?
Which division increases heart rate and dilates the pupils during stress?
A person is startled and their heart races. Which division is responsible?
Which division speeds up the heart and diverts blood to skeletal muscles during danger?
Which part of the nervous system is activated during an emergency, releasing norepinephrine and epinephrine?
Which division is dominant when a person is frightened or exercising intensely?
Which autonomic division increases the breathing rate and slows digestion during stress?
The fight-or-flight response is controlled by which division of the nervous system?

questions.why: The sympathetic division of the autonomic nervous system produces the fight-or-flight response: faster heart rate, dilated pupils, faster breathing, and slowed digestion.
questions.deep: Sympathetic = fight or flight (energy used). Parasympathetic = rest and digest (energy saved): slows the heart, increases digestion. Both are parts of the autonomic nervous system, which controls involuntary functions. The somatic system controls voluntary skeletal muscle.

variants.stem: Which organ filters blood and removes old or damaged red blood cells?
Which lymphatic organ stores platelets and filters blood?
Which organ, located in the upper left abdomen, filters blood and helps fight infection?
Which organ recycles iron from old red blood cells as it filters blood?
Which organ contains white pulp and red pulp?
Which organ acts as a blood filter and blood reservoir in the lymphatic system?
Old red blood cells are destroyed in which lymphatic organ?
Which organ filters blood rather than lymph?

questions.why: The spleen filters blood, removes old or damaged red blood cells, recycles iron, and stores platelets and white blood cells.
questions.deep: Lymph nodes filter lymph; the spleen filters blood. The thymus is where T cells mature. The spleen sits in the upper left abdomen, behind the stomach. People can live without a spleen, though they are more prone to certain infections.

variants.stem: The metric prefix kilo- means how many of the base unit?
How many meters are in one kilometer?
One kilogram equals how many grams?
One kiloliter is equal to how many liters?
Which number does the prefix kilo- represent as a multiplier?
How many watts are in one kilowatt?
Which number of base units equals one kilo-unit?
A kilogram is how many times larger than a gram?

questions.why: The metric prefix kilo- means one thousand, so 1 kilogram = 1,000 grams and 1 kilometer = 1,000 meters.
questions.deep: Prefix ladder (largest to smallest): kilo (1,000), hecto (100), deka (10), base unit, deci (0.1), centi (0.01), milli (0.001). Going from a larger unit to a smaller unit, multiply; going from smaller to larger, divide.

variants.stem: A scatter plot shows that as the number of hours studied increases, test scores also increase. What type of relationship is this?
Data show that students who study more hours tend to score higher on tests. Which term describes this relationship?
As one variable increases, the other variable also increases. This is called a:
A scatter plot slopes upward from left to right. What relationship does it show?
Higher study hours are associated with higher scores. Which statement describes the relationship?
On a graph, as x increases, y increases. This shows:
Which type of correlation exists when both variables rise together?
Test scores go up as study time goes up. This is an example of a:

questions.why: When both variables increase together, the data show a positive correlation, and a scatter plot slopes upward from left to right.
questions.deep: Positive correlation: both rise together (slope up). Negative (inverse) correlation: one rises as the other falls (slope down). No correlation: no pattern. Correlation does not by itself prove that one variable causes the other.

questions.why: A larger sample reduces the influence of random variation, so the results are more likely to represent the whole population and be reliable.
questions.deep: A bigger sample does not guarantee the hypothesis is true and does not remove bias (a biased sample stays biased) or the need for a control group. Repeating trials and using enough subjects both improve reliability.
